Hastily
hās'tĭ-lĭ
adv. (in haste; quickly; also, rashly, without due deliberation)
Old French haste, speed. The Authorized Version uses the word both for a summons that cannot wait and for the rashness Solomon warns against.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sometimes haste is God's timing: “Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh” (Gen 41:14). After thirteen years, the change took an hour. Sometimes the absence of haste is God's method: “the LORD left those nations, without driving them out hastily; neither delivered he them into the hand of Joshua” (Jdg 2:23), and Exodus explains why — lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply against thee: by little and little I will drive them out. Sometimes haste is panic: Abimelech, with a millstone in his skull, “called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer” to run him through, so that men would not say a woman slew him (Jdg 9:54), a man managing his reputation with his last breath. And sometimes haste is the news itself: “the man came in hastily, and told Eli” (1Sa 4:14) that Israel was fled, his sons were dead, and the ark of God was taken. Over all of it stands Solomon's rule for the tongue and the temper: he that hasteth with his feet sinneth, and, be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines hastily as in haste; with speed or quickness; speedily; nimbly; and also rashly, precipitately, without due reflection.

expand to see more

HASTILY, adv. In haste; with speed or quickness; speedily; nimbly.

2. Rashly; precipitately; without due reflection.

3. Passionately; under sudden excitement of passion.

Key Scripture

Gen 41:14 — "Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh."

Jdg 2:23 — "Therefore the LORD left those nations, without driving them out hastily; neither delivered he them into the hand of Joshua."

Pro 19:2 — "Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth."

Modern Corruption

Speed is treated as a virtue in itself, and Scripture consistently distinguishes the haste that obeys a summons from the haste that outruns knowledge.

expand to see more

Judges 2:23 says something a results-driven age finds nearly incomprehensible: the LORD left those nations, without driving them out hastily. He could have emptied Canaan in a week; He said He would do it by little and little, and gave two reasons — that the land not become desolate and the wild beasts multiply, and that Israel might be proved and taught war. Sanctification runs on the same principle, and it is the reason God does not remove every sin from a believer at conversion: the ground could not carry it, and the man would learn nothing. Meanwhile Proverbs draws the line on the other side: he that hasteth with his feet sinneth; the thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness, but of every one that is hasty only to want; be not rash with thy mouth; he that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him. The haste Scripture blesses is obedience to a summons — the shepherds came with haste to Bethlehem, Zacchaeus made haste and came down, David ran toward the giant. The haste it condemns is the haste that outruns knowledge: the vow, the answer, the purchase, the appointment of a novice to office, the marriage entered on a fortnight's acquaintance. The test is not the speed but whether the man knows what he is doing. Joseph came out of the dungeon hastily because God's hour had struck after thirteen years of not striking.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ruwts (H7323), to run; mahar (H4116), to hasten, to be rash; 'uwts (H213), to press, to be hasty — the verb of Proverbs 19:2.

expand to see more

Hebrew ruwts (H7323) — to run; they brought Joseph hastily out of the dungeon; Genesis 41:14.

Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, and so to be rash or impetuous; be not rash with thy mouth; Ecclesiastes 5:2, Proverbs 25:8.

Hebrew 'uwts (H213) — to press, urge, be hasty; he that hasteth with his feet sinneth; Proverbs 19:2, 21:5.

Usage

"“They brought him hastily out of the dungeon” — thirteen years, then one hour."

"“Without driving them out hastily” — by little and little, and for a reason."

"“He that hasteth with his feet sinneth” — the haste that outruns knowledge."
